messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Khalid's Story

Khalid was thirty-eight when his brother Rami died in a convenience store robbery gone wrong. It happened at 11:47 p.m. on a Tuesday night—a time Khalid would come to dread with an almost physical revulsion. Khalid had been working late at the McDonald's on Atlantic Avenue when Rami texted asking if he wanted coffee before bed. Khalid said yes. He was in the break room when the call came through from the police. Rami had walked in on two men with a gun. There was shouting, a struggle Khalid would never fully understand, and then a single shot that echoed through the store and into Khalid's life forever. By the time Khalid arrived at the hospital, his brother was already gone. The officer who met him kept saying how quick it was, as if speed could soften the fact of it.

The first weeks after the funeral passed in a fog of practical tasks and numb condolences. But as autumn turned to winter, something shifted. Khalid began to notice that around 11 p.m., his body would tense without his conscious permission. His shoulders would bunch up toward his ears. His palms would sweat. He found himself checking the locks on his apartment door repeatedly, moving from room to room as if searching for something he couldn't name. By the time the clock approached midnight, he would be in bed with all the lights off, his phone clutched in his hand, waiting for the hour to pass. He had come to believe that danger accumulated in the dark hours, that the world became fundamentally unsafe after the sun went down. This temporal threat felt almost as real as a physical presence in the room.

The triggers that activated this hypervigilance extended beyond the clock. Any loud noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the sharp beep of the microwave in the break room at work—would send a jolt of adrenaline through his chest. His coworkers had started to notice. Last month, when the manager, Tony, had called out a mistake Khalid made while taking an order, Khalid had flinched so violently that he'd knocked over a stack of napkin dispensers. The criticism itself wasn't harsh—just routine correction—but it triggered the same suffocating sense of danger that the loud noises did. Being corrected had become indistinguishable from being threatened. Khalid couldn't quite explain why a simple "Hey, you rang that up wrong" felt like an accusation, like proof that he was failing to protect himself or anyone else. The connection was irrational, he knew, but the fear was absolute.

This hyperalertness to threat had colonized his entire life. Khalid had narrowed his world to a handful of locations where he felt even remotely safe: his apartment, his sister's house, and a small section of the parking lot at work where he could see the exit. Anywhere else—the grocery store, the bus, a restaurant—felt permeable and dangerous. He had stopped going to the mosque he'd attended for twenty years because the crowd, the echoing space, the unpredictability of when someone might speak loudly or move suddenly, all of it felt intolerable. When something took longer than expected—a delayed bus, a slow checkout line—his mind would immediately leap to catastrophe. Something bad was happening, or about to. The delay itself became evidence of threat. Three years had passed since Rami's death, and Khalid's world had only gotten smaller. He'd called his sister last week and finally admitted he needed help. He was tired of being afraid. He was tired of the way his body had become a prison, locked into the same moment of terror over and over again.
